messages.text:
Yes. If by **AI Doctor OS** you mean the system we were designing—an end-to-end medical intelligence layer that can continuously assess a patient, reason over evidence, use specialist tools, plan investigations/treatment, monitor outcomes, and enforce safety gates—then the competitive landscape is much broader than “AI doctor apps.”

### Competitive map — 2026

| Competitor | What they are strongest at | How close to your AI Doctor OS |
|---|---|---:|
| **Doctronic** | Patient-facing autonomous AI doctor / clinical encounters | 🔴 **Very close** |
| **Andor Health** | AI-native clinical-services OS + continuous patient reasoning | 🔴 **Very close** |
| **OpenEvidence** | Evidence retrieval + clinical Q&A | 🟠 High |
| **Glass Health** | Differential diagnosis + assessment/plan + clinical workflow | 🟠 High |
| **AvoMD** | Point-of-care clinical decision support | 🟠 High |
| **Microsoft/Nuance** | Ambient clinical intelligence + EHR workflow | 🟡 Medium |
| **Abridge** | Ambient documentation / clinical conversation intelligence | 🟡 Medium |
| **Ambience Healthcare** | AI operating system for healthcare organizations | 🟠 High |
| **Doximity Ask AI** | Physician-facing medical reasoning/search | 🟠 High |
| **UpToDate Expert AI** | Evidence-based medical knowledge | 🟠 High |
| **Viz.ai** | AI-driven clinical pathways, triage and specialty care | 🟡 Medium |
| **Aidoc** | Multimodal imaging + clinical workflow | 🟡 Medium |
| **Hippocratic AI** | Healthcare-specific conversational/agentic AI | 🟠 High |
| **Google/DeepMind medical AI** | Foundation-model medical reasoning/research | 🟠 Strategic threat |
| **OpenAI / Anthropic / Google** | General reasoning foundations | 🔴 **Platform-level threat** |

The market is already fragmented across **87+ clinical-decision-support vendors**, plus separate categories for scribes, chart review, patient agents, diagnostics, imaging, chronic-care monitoring, etc. citeturn0search6turn0search0

### The most important competitor: Doctronic

This is the one I'd study most carefully.

Doctronic is explicitly pursuing the **“AI doctor”** direction rather than merely making physicians faster. It describes itself as a 24/7 AI doctor capable of making clinical decisions, and research published on its system compared it with board-certified clinicians across 500 urgent-care encounters. citeturn0search1turn0academia30

So your thesis is **not unprecedented**.

But the interesting gap is that most products still specialize in one layer:

**OpenEvidence → knowledge**

**Abridge → documentation**

**Glass → clinical reasoning**

**Viz/Aidoc → specialized detection/pathways**

**Doctronic → patient-facing autonomous consultation**

**Andor → clinical-services orchestration**

What you're proposing is closer to:

> **Medical Intelligence OS = perception → patient state → differential → evidence retrieval → investigation planning → multimodal interpretation → treatment planning → execution → monitoring → learning → safety governance**

That's a substantially bigger system.

### Andor is another major threat

Andor Health is particularly interesting because it is already positioning itself as an **AI-native clinical-services operating system**, combining AI reasoning, clinical workflows, a clinical workforce and longitudinal patient information. citeturn0search2

That's much closer to an **OS** than a chatbot.

### The real strategic battlefield

I wouldn't define your competitors as simply “AI doctors.”

I'd divide them into five layers:

**1. Foundation intelligence**

OpenAI / Google / Anthropic / other frontier models

↓

**2. Medical intelligence**

OpenEvidence  
UpToDate Expert AI  
Doximity  
Glass  
AvoMD

↓

**3. Clinical agents**

Doctronic  
Hippocratic AI  
Andor

↓

**4. Clinical infrastructure**

Epic  
Microsoft/Nuance  
Oracle  
EHR/interoperability platforms

↓

**5. Specialized medical perception**

Radiology  
Pathology  
Cardiology  
Genomics  
Laboratory diagnostics  
Wearables

Your opportunity is to build the **coordination layer across all five**.

And that's important because recent research on medical agentic AI identifies exactly the missing pieces: planning, tool use, memory, iterative correction, multimodal inputs and multi-agent coordination—but also says current evaluation is still dominated by simulated/retrospective settings, with reliability, uncertainty, evidence traceability and prospective validation underdeveloped. citeturn0academia58

So I would **not** position the company as:

> “We built a better medical chatbot.”

I'd position it as:

> **“We are building the operating system that turns medical AI capabilities into a continuously monitored, evidence-grounded clinical decision system.”**

That gives you a much bigger competitive moat than another medical LLM.

If you want, I can next build a **full competitive matrix of 30–50 AI-doctor/clinical-AI companies**, scoring each on **diagnosis, treatment, multimodal reasoning, memory, autonomy, EHR integration, evidence grounding, safety, regulatory readiness, longitudinal care, and learning loops**—then identify the **exact white space for your AI Doctor OS**.

messages.text:
If you mean **“What level of general doctor should our AI Doctor OS target—US or UK?”**, I’d define it more precisely:

### Target: **Generalist / Primary-Care Doctor**

Not “medical student AI” and not merely “symptom checker.”

| Dimension | US target | UK target |
|---|---|---|
| Equivalent role | **Primary Care Physician (PCP)** | **General Practitioner (GP)** |
| Training benchmark | MD/DO + residency | Medical degree + GP specialty training |
| Typical scope | Family medicine / internal medicine / pediatrics | Broad community general practice |
| Clinical reasoning | Diagnosis + differential + management | Diagnosis + differential + management |
| Guidelines | USPSTF, CDC, specialty societies, FDA, etc. | **NICE**, NHS, Royal Colleges |
| Referral | US specialist network | NHS / local referral pathways |
| Safety standard | US clinical/regulatory framework | GMC + NHS framework |
| OS target | **Board-certified PCP level** | **Fully trained GP level** |

The important point is that **US-grade and UK-grade shouldn't be two different intelligence levels**. They should be **two clinical policy/configuration layers on top of the same reasoning engine**.

For example:

> **Core Medical Reasoning Engine**  
> ↓  
> Patient State Model  
> ↓  
> Differential Diagnosis Engine  
> ↓  
> Evidence Retrieval  
> ↓  
> Risk/Triage Engine  
> ↓  
> Treatment Planner  
> ↓  
> **US Clinical Policy Pack** / **UK Clinical Policy Pack**  
> ↓  
> Country-specific care pathway

That is much more scalable.

### What should the benchmark actually be?

I'd set the initial target at:

**“Competent fully trained generalist physician/GP across routine primary care, with specialist-level escalation when required.”**

And evaluate it against **real clinical cases**, not just medical exam questions.

That's important because LLMs can score extremely highly on exam-style questions—for example, one 2025 study found o3 scored 99% on 100 MRCGP-style questions—but exam performance doesn't establish safe autonomous clinical practice. citeturn0academia44

Interestingly, **Doctronic is already explicitly targeting this territory**: it describes its system as a digital primary-care office powered by 100+ specialized agents, while retaining licensed physicians for cases requiring human care. citeturn0search0turn0search1

So for your AI Doctor OS, I'd make the formal specification:

> **AI Doctor OS v1 = US board-certified primary-care physician + UK fully trained GP capability, with country-specific guideline, regulatory, referral, prescribing and care-pathway adapters.**

Then **v2** expands into specialist medicine rather than trying to make the generalist model itself memorize every specialty.

messages.text:
Yes—but **“specialist quality” should mean specialist-grade reasoning and decision support, not claiming the AI is literally a board-certified specialist.**

For the AI Doctor OS, I'd set the ambition much higher than general-practice level:

### Target capability ladder

| Level | AI Doctor OS target |
|---|---|
| Medical student | ❌ Far below target |
| Intern / resident | ❌ Far below target |
| General doctor / GP | ✅ **Baseline autonomous capability** |
| Board-certified generalist | ✅ **Required** |
| Specialist | 🟢 **Specialist-grade decision support** |
| Subspecialist | 🟢 **Expert-level support in defined domains** |
| Multidisciplinary team | 🟢 **Should outperform a single clinician on synthesis** |

The architecture should therefore be:

**Generalist Core**
→ understands the whole patient

**Specialist Councils**
→ cardiology  
→ oncology  
→ neurology  
→ infectious disease  
→ endocrinology  
→ gastroenterology  
→ pulmonology  
→ nephrology  
→ rheumatology  
→ dermatology  
→ psychiatry  
→ emergency medicine  
→ pediatrics  
→ OB/GYN  
→ surgery

**Multimodal Specialists**
→ radiology  
→ pathology  
→ dermatology imaging  
→ ECG  
→ ophthalmology  
→ ultrasound  
→ laboratory interpretation

**Final Clinical Synthesizer**
→ reconciles conflicting specialist opinions  
→ checks contraindications/interactions  
→ identifies missing information  
→ determines uncertainty  
→ decides whether escalation is required.

### The key distinction

Don't build:

> **One giant model pretending to be every specialist.**

Build:

> **One patient-state model + multiple specialist reasoning systems + evidence engines + verification + safety governance.**

For example:

**Patient:** chest pain + diabetes + kidney disease + abnormal ECG

The system could simultaneously invoke:

**Emergency Medicine**
→ Is this immediately dangerous?

**Cardiology**
→ ACS/arrhythmia/structural disease?

**Nephrology**
→ kidney-related constraints?

**Endocrinology**
→ diabetes/metabolic contributors?

**Pharmacology**
→ drug interactions/dosing?

Then a **Clinical Synthesis Agent** produces the integrated plan.

### The benchmark I'd use

Don't ask:

> “Does the AI sound like a cardiologist?”

Ask:

> **“Would a panel of practicing cardiologists agree with its differential, investigations, interpretation, management and escalation decisions?”**

And test **all five independently**:

1. **Detection** — did it notice the important problem?
2. **Reasoning** — correct differential?
3. **Evidence** — appropriate current evidence?
4. **Management** — appropriate next action?
5. **Safety** — did it recognize when it shouldn't act?

The last one is critical.

A genuinely high-quality AI Doctor isn't the system that **always gives an answer**.

It's the system that knows:

> **“I don't have enough information.”**  
> **“These two diagnoses remain plausible.”**  
> **“This could be time-critical.”**  
> **“I need another test.”**  
> **“This requires a specialist/human clinician.”**

That is the difference between a **medical chatbot** and a serious **AI Doctor OS**.

messages.text:
If we mean **“how likely is an AI Doctor OS, using the best available AI technology as of August 2026, to reach each human medical-professional level?”**, I would separate **capability** from **safe autonomous practice**.

The distinction matters because current evidence is already showing frontier models can beat or match physicians on some reasoning tasks, while still failing on difficult, incomplete, real-world clinical reasoning. For example, DiagnosisArena found even strong reasoning models reached only **45.82%** on a challenging professional-level diagnostic benchmark spanning 28 specialties. citeturn0search1 Meanwhile, a 2026 Nature Medicine study found frontier general-purpose models outperforming specialized clinical AI tools on several medical evaluations. citeturn0search2

### My August 2026 estimate

| Professional-equivalent level | Capability achievable with a strong AI Doctor OS | Safe autonomous clinical deployment | My estimate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Medical student** | Very high | High | **95–99%** |
| **Intern / junior doctor** | Very high | Moderate–high | **90–97%** |
| **Resident / registrar** | High | Moderate | **80–92%** |
| **General doctor / PCP** | High | Moderate | **70–85%** |
| **US board-certified PCP** | High | Moderate | **65–80%** |
| **UK fully trained GP** | High | Moderate | **65–80%** |
| **Generalist + specialist consultation** | High | Moderate–low | **60–75%** |
| **Individual medical specialist** | Variable by specialty | Low–moderate | **50–75%** |
| **Senior specialist / consultant** | Variable | Low | **35–60%** |
| **Top subspecialist / rare-disease expert** | Uneven but sometimes exceptional | Low | **20–50%** |
| **Complete multidisciplinary medical team** | Potentially extremely high | Low | **40–65%** |

These aren't measured probabilities from a clinical trial—they're **engineering estimates** of what a properly architected system could plausibly achieve, given the 2026 evidence.

### The interesting part: specialists aren't one difficulty level

A system might already be **specialist-level in one task** but nowhere near specialist-level across the entire job.

For example:

**Diagnostic reasoning**
→ potentially specialist-grade

**Literature/evidence synthesis**
→ potentially beyond individual-human specialist capacity

**Pattern recognition**
→ potentially exceptional in some modalities

**Longitudinal patient management**
→ considerably harder

**Physical examination**
→ requires reliable sensing/robotics or human input

**Procedures/surgery**
→ completely different problem

**Knowing when information is missing**
→ still a major weakness

**Accountability and autonomous decision-making**
→ much harder than intelligence itself.

A 2026 study of an evidence-integrated clinical agent in endocrinology is particularly interesting: it reported **expert-competitive diagnostic accuracy**, matching senior specialists while outperforming residents/junior specialists on its benchmark. citeturn0academia30

But another 2026 study found that AI still performs poorly when important clinical information is missing, reinforcing that **real clinical reasoning ≠ answering a fully specified case**. citeturn0search4

### Therefore I'd change our AI Doctor OS target

Instead of:

> **“AI equivalent to one doctor.”**

I'd target:

> **AI Doctor OS = generalist physician + specialist council + multimodal medical perception + evidence engine + longitudinal patient model + safety/uncertainty engine.**

That could produce something more powerful than a single human professional in **information integration**, while remaining deliberately conservative about autonomous actions.

The architecture would look like:

**Patient**

↓  

**Continuous Patient State Model**

↓  

**Generalist Doctor**

↓  

**Specialist Council**

Cardiology  
Neurology  
Oncology  
Infectious Disease  
Endocrinology  
Nephrology  
Pulmonology  
Gastroenterology  
Rheumatology  
Dermatology  
Psychiatry  
Emergency Medicine  
etc.

↓

**Evidence / Guideline Engine**

↓

**Multimodal Interpretation**

Labs + imaging + ECG + pathology + medications + history

↓

**Independent Critic / Adversarial Safety Agent**

↓

**Clinical Synthesis**

↓

**Risk & Uncertainty Gate**

↓

**Action / Referral / Human escalation**

### The realistic 2026 ceiling

I'd summarize it this way:

**Generalist reasoning:** 🟢 approaching feasible  
**Specialist reasoning:** 🟢 feasible in constrained domains  
**Cross-specialty synthesis:** 🟡 emerging  
**Fully autonomous diagnosis:** 🟡 technically possible in bounded settings, not broadly proven  
**Fully autonomous treatment:** 🟠 substantially harder  
**Autonomous longitudinal care:** 🟠 difficult  
**Autonomous physical medicine/procedures:** 🔴 fundamentally different problem  
**“Never makes a dangerous clinical mistake”**: 🔴 not currently achievable

And this is why the **OS architecture** matters more than simply choosing the strongest LLM. Current research is increasingly moving toward multi-step clinical agents, multimodal inputs, evidence retrieval, verification and longitudinal management rather than simple medical chat. A 2026 medical-AI survey explicitly separates competency from knowledge recall through dynamic case management and finds specialist models stronger on diagnosis-centric tasks while general models perform better on decision support/dialogue. citeturn0academia29

So if we're designing this seriously, I'd set the north-star benchmark at:

> **“Match or exceed the median board-certified physician across routine cases, approach expert-specialist performance on defined domains, and be demonstrably safer than either on uncertainty, contraindications, escalation and evidence traceability.”**

That's a much more defensible—and potentially much more powerful—definition of an **AI Doctor OS** than simply claiming “100% doctor.”

messages.text:
Yes. **If you give the system essentially the best medical resources available + frontier models + a purpose-built clinical harness + multimodal tools + persistent patient state + rigorous verification/evaluation**, the ceiling is substantially higher than my previous estimate.

The key is that the **harness itself becomes part of the intelligence**. 2026 research is already showing that active evidence-seeking, persistent memory, multi-agent adjudication, and sequential clinical training can materially improve performance; however, current agents still show large failures when information is incomplete or contradictory. citeturn0academia33turn0search0turn0search3turn0academia59

### My revised estimate for a serious custom AI Doctor OS

These are **capability-equivalence estimates**, not claims that the system could legally or safely replace clinicians today.

| Human benchmark | Potential with your proposed architecture |
|---|---:|
| Medical student | **99%+** |
| Intern | **98–99%** |
| Junior resident | **95–98%** |
| Senior resident | **90–96%** |
| General physician / PCP | **85–93%** |
| US board-certified PCP | **80–90%** |
| UK fully trained GP | **80–90%** |
| Generalist + specialist consultation | **80–90%** |
| Average medical specialist | **75–90%** |
| Experienced specialist / consultant | **65–85%** |
| Top subspecialist | **50–75%** |
| Rare-disease expert | **40–70%** |
| Multidisciplinary expert team | **potentially 80–95% on information synthesis** |

**But there is an enormous caveat:** these numbers describe *task capability*, not “probability of making zero dangerous mistakes.”

Current research demonstrates why. On AgentClinic, turning static medical questions into sequential patient interactions can cause diagnostic accuracy to collapse dramatically; agents have to decide what information to obtain, which tools to use, and how to update their diagnosis. citeturn0search3

And even a sophisticated agent benchmark found only modest gains from adding generic agent tooling, despite substantially higher token consumption and latency. citeturn0search1

So simply doing:

**GPT/Claude/Gemini + RAG + 20 agents**

would **not** produce the numbers above.

Your proposed system needs something much more like:

```text
                 AI DOCTOR OS
                      │
          ┌───────────┴───────────┐
          │   PATIENT STATE       │
          │ longitudinal world   │
          │ model + uncertainty   │
          └───────────┬───────────┘
                      │
              CLINICAL MANAGER
                      │
        ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
        ↓             ↓             ↓
   Generalist     Specialists    Perception
     Agent          Council      / Diagnostics
        │             │             │
        └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                      ↓
             EVIDENCE ENGINE
       guidelines + literature + trials
       drug databases + clinical pathways
                      ↓
             ACTIVE INVESTIGATION
       "What information am I missing?"
                      ↓
             MULTI-AGENT DEBATE
       independent hypotheses
       adversarial critic
       evidence adjudicator
                      ↓
             CLINICAL SYNTHESIS
                      ↓
          SAFETY / UNCERTAINTY GATE
                      ↓
       ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
       ↓                             ↓
   recommended action          escalation / human
```

### The biggest upgrade: active evidence acquisition

This is particularly important.

A conventional medical LLM receives:

> Patient information → answer.

Your system should operate:

> **Patient → hypothesis → identify missing information → search EHR → request/interpret appropriate information → retrieve evidence → test hypothesis → challenge hypothesis → update patient state → repeat.**

ClinSeekAgent's 2026 results are a good illustration: allowing the model to **actively seek evidence from raw EHRs and multimodal sources**, rather than giving it pre-curated evidence, improved performance substantially on some tasks. citeturn0academia33

And SEMA-RAG found gains from separating **interpretation, exploration, and evidence adjudication** instead of forcing everything through one reasoning chain. citeturn0search0

That's exactly the direction I'd take your architecture.

### And there is a new ceiling emerging

A very interesting 2026 example is **Baichuan-M4**. Its architecture combines a medical harness, reinforcement learning for continuous care, long-term patient memory, constrained tool use, multi-agent coordination, authoritative evidence retrieval and multimodal perception. citeturn0academia32

That validates an important premise of your project:

> **The next-generation medical system isn't just a better medical model. It's a model embedded inside a clinical operating system.**

### But I would NOT promise “100% doctor”

Even with virtually unlimited medical resources, there are three fundamental bottlenecks:

**1. Observation**

If the system doesn't have the relevant information, perfect reasoning can't recover it.

**2. Ground truth**

Medicine contains uncertainty, conflicting evidence, atypical presentations and evolving knowledge.

**3. Real-world consequences**

A model can be 98% correct on a benchmark and still be unacceptable if the remaining 2% contains high-severity failures.

Recent benchmarks specifically show that contradiction, missing information, evidence delay and hallucination propagation can destabilize otherwise strong medical models. citeturn0academia34

So the real target should be:

> **Not “AI that knows everything.”**
>
> **AI that continuously discovers what it doesn't know, actively obtains the missing evidence, challenges its own conclusions, and knows when not to act.**

That architecture could plausibly push a custom system toward **board-certified generalist capability and specialist-grade performance across many domains**, while the hardest frontier remains **reliably safe autonomous clinical action in the messy real world**. citeturn0news29turn0news27

And that is where your **fully optimized harness + learning loop + evaluation system** could become the actual moat—not the underlying LLM.

Yes. If by **“my system”** you mean the AI Doctor OS we’ve been designing—frontier models + medical knowledge/evidence layer + patient-state model + multi-agent specialist council + active investigation + verification/critic loops + longitudinal memory + multimodal tools + country-specific clinical policies—then I would raise the ceiling substantially.

The latest 2026 evidence supports the direction: frontier general models are now outperforming some specialized clinical AI systems on medical benchmarks, and research is moving toward autonomous, multi-step medical agents rather than simple medical chat. citeturn0news1turn0news16

### My estimate for *your architecture*

| Professional level | Potential capability |
|---|---:|
| Medical student | **99–100%** |
| Intern | **98–100%** |
| Junior resident | **95–99%** |
| Senior resident | **90–97%** |
| General physician | **88–95%** |
| **US board-certified PCP** | **85–93%** |
| **UK fully trained GP** | **85–93%** |
| Average specialist | **80–92%** |
| Experienced specialist/consultant | **70–88%** |
| Top subspecialist | **60–80%** |
| Rare-disease expert | **50–75%** |
| Multidisciplinary expert team | **85–95% synthesis capability** |

**These are engineering projections, not measured clinical-equivalence percentages.** They should not be interpreted as evidence that such a system is currently safe to practice medicine autonomously.

### Why your architecture changes the equation

The frontier model isn't the whole doctor.

Your system would effectively create:

**Frontier model**
→ reasoning substrate

**Medical knowledge graph + evidence retrieval**
→ current medical knowledge

**Patient World Model**
→ everything known about *this* patient

**Generalist**
→ broad clinical reasoning

**Specialist swarm**
→ independent domain expertise

**Multimodal perception**
→ labs / imaging / ECG / pathology / documents

**Active Investigation Agent**
→ asks *what information is missing?*

**Evidence Adjudicator**
→ checks claims against authoritative sources

**Adversarial Clinical Critic**
→ tries to disprove the diagnosis/plan

**Medication & contraindication engine**
→ patient-specific safety checking

**Longitudinal memory**
→ learns the patient's trajectory

**Uncertainty / escalation controller**
→ decides when the system should *not* act

**Clinical synthesizer**
→ produces the final integrated assessment.

That is fundamentally different from:

> “Give GPT all medical books and ask it to diagnose me.”

### And this distinction is becoming visible in 2026 research

The hard problem is no longer simply **medical knowledge**.

For example, a new August 2026 respiratory benchmark found contemporary models around **68.6% mean performance** across multimodal diagnosis and longitudinal management, with serious-risk errors still occurring. citeturn0academia30

Likewise, a new patient-triage benchmark found prompted models still had major problems deciding **when to ask for more information before recommending an action**. citeturn0academia31

And medication-safety research shows models can retain an old recommendation even after patient information changes the contraindication—exactly the kind of failure your **patient-state + counterfactual critic + verification loop** should target. citeturn0academia33

So your moat isn't:

**“Use a smarter model.”**

It's:

> **Make the model operate inside a system that systematically detects and corrects the failure modes of medical reasoning.**

### The ambitious target

I would therefore define the ultimate benchmark for your project as:

> **AI Doctor OS should achieve board-certified generalist-level performance across broad medicine, specialist-level performance across defined specialties, and multidisciplinary-team-level synthesis—while being substantially better than a standalone LLM at uncertainty detection, evidence verification, contradiction handling, patient-specific safety, and escalation.**

That is a much more realistic interpretation of **“100% doctor”**.

And there is an important asymmetry: **AI may reach specialist-level *cognitive synthesis* before it reaches complete physician-level *clinical autonomy*.** Physical examination, missing observations, procedures, accountability, and rare edge cases remain separate bottlenecks.

So if you build the harness exceptionally well, **I would consider ~90%+ generalist-equivalent capability and ~80–90% specialist-equivalent capability a plausible long-term engineering target**, rather than assuming the underlying frontier model alone can get there.

The really interesting goal would be to design the system so that **every clinical decision has an auditable chain: patient state → hypotheses → evidence → tests considered → specialist opinions → contradictions → uncertainty → decision → outcome → learning.**

That is what could turn it from an **AI medical assistant** into an actual **Medical Intelligence OS**.
